paras: The Winston jail riot took place on the night of August 11, 1895, in Winston, North Carolina, when an armed crowd of Black residents gathered at the jail to protect a Black prisoner, Arthur Tuttle, from a rumored lynching and was scattered by volleys from the militia and deputies. Several of the crowd were wounded and at least one later died; about fifty Black men were jailed and prosecuted, and hundreds left the town. The dispatch ran nationally, often under the heading "race war".

Tuttle was on trial before Judge Brown for the murder of Officer M. M. Vickers, shot on May 18 when police tried to clear a sidewalk crowd, according to police testimony. The Raleigh News and Observer wrote that Black residents "favor Tuttle" and later reported that his brother had been killed by a policeman, Hasting, who was acquitted.

Word was given out in the Black churches that a crowd of whites meant to lynch Tuttle; trial testimony traced it to his brother Bob, who rose after a service at the Methodist Episcopal (colored) church and asked for help. Men armed with pistols and guns, numbered at about 150, 300 or "some 800", marched to the jail and stayed for hours. Mayor Eugene Gray, Sheriff McArthur, two lawyers and Judge Brown assured them that Tuttle was safe, and the mayor sent the police chief with one of them to check a report of horses tied in the pine woods.

The crowd agreed to leave if twenty men guarded the jail, but many stayed after the guard was posted. On the judge's order the sheriff called out the Forsyth Riflemen and swore in deputies to arrest those who would not disperse. In the officials' account the crowd fired first, striking several officers with birdshot, and the riflemen answered with volleys; about 150 shots were exchanged. The crowd fled carrying its wounded, and fourteen men were arrested.

Judge Brown charged the grand jury the next day, and a Gatling gun arrived from Charlotte while the town obtained a hundred rifles and swore in sixty police. Tuttle was convicted of second-degree murder on August 13 and sentenced to twenty-five years. By August 15 fifty Black men were jailed and over a hundred true bills returned; forty were arraigned for unlawful assembly and concealed weapons.

Micajah Watts, called a leader, got six months on the county roads, and a special term ordered by Governor Elias Carr opened on August 19 with six guilty pleas; no report of its final verdicts was found. That day the correspondent reported that "another of the negro rioters, who was shot," had died. More than two hundred Black residents left, many without their wages, and tobacco factories ran short of hands. Dave Koontz, with a finger shot off and a leg wound, was jailed in September, saying he had been a spectator.

White papers from Maine to Arizona carried the Winston dispatch, giving the officials' account of who fired first as fact. Headlines ran from "Negroes Were Determined to Protect One of Their Race From Lynching" in Topeka to "Carolina Race War" in Fort Worth, which credited the riflemen's "Well- Directed Volleys." The Arizona Republican headed it "A Lively Battle", and the Norfolk Virginian spoke of quelling "the Disturbing Colored Element."

The News and Observer headlined "A Bloody Race Riot Narrowly Averted", and its trial report, also printed in the Richmond Times, called the crowd's stand "remarkably foolish". The Kansas State Ledger, a Topeka weekly addressing colored readers, alone condemned it, calling it an attempt by armed white men to lynch, defeated by colored men "stoutly resisting." No Black newspaper's account appears in the coverage.

A train passenger quoted by the News and Observer and the Scotland Neck Democrat said Friends returning from High Point had been taken for a lynching band. Both said the crowd fired as people were about to leave, not after refusing to go. First reports said no one was killed; the later death was called "another", though no earlier one appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Winston jail riot
bases: The violence against Black people reported is the Forsyth Riflemen and sworn deputies, called out by the sheriff on the judge's order, firing volleys into an armed Black crowd at the jail, followed by mass arrest and prosecution; no white mob is reported to have appeared (A1, A5, A27).

The wire dispatch (A1, A5), the Raleigh paper's own Winston specials (A4, A18, A27) and the Scotland Neck Democrat (A23) agree on the armed gathering at the jail, the exchange of fire and the arrests, though they differ on cause, size and who fired first.

accounts.label: Wire dispatch from Winston
accounts.gist: A report in the Black churches that Tuttle would be lynched brought 150 (elsewhere 300 or 800) armed Black men to the jail; they stayed despite assurances and a guard of twenty, fired on the officers, and were scattered by militia volleys; 14 were arrested.

accounts.label: Train passenger (Raleigh News & Observer)
accounts.gist: People returning from the Friends meeting at High Point rode through town after midnight and were taken for a lynching mob; after the mayor rescinded the judge's order and told everyone to disperse, the crowd fired as officers and soldiers started to leave, wounding the sheriff.

accounts.label: Scotland Neck Democrat
accounts.gist: A company of Friends passing through from High Point caused the alarm; the crowd agreed to leave if a guard was posted, but 'when about to leave' fired into the officers.

accounts.label: Trial testimony (Mayor Gray; examination at the special term)
accounts.gist: The crowd feared Tuttle would be lynched by people from the country and had heard of horses tied in the pine woods, which the mayor had the police chief check; Bob Tuttle had raised the alarm in church.

accounts.label: Kansas State Ledger editorial
accounts.gist: Armed white men attempted to lynch a colored man and were stopped by colored men resisting; a few on each side were shot, none seriously.

framing.detail: The national wire ran under headlines such as 'Blacks and Whites Shoot' with the deck 'Negroes Were Determined to Protect One of Their Race From Lynching', and 'Meant Business'.

The Fort Worth Gazette headed it 'Carolina Race War' with 'State Riflemen Scatter a Large Mob of Negroes by Several Well-Directed Volleys', and the Norfolk Virginian spoke of quelling 'the Disturbing Colored Element'.
The Arizona Republican made light of it as 'A Lively Battle' in which 'Negroes and Militiamen Enjoy a Scrimmage'.

The Raleigh News and Observer headlined 'From Church to Jail / A Bloody Race Riot Narrowly Averted' and, with the Richmond Times, reported the trial testimony as showing the crowd's 'folly' and 'remarkably foolish' stubbornness.

The Kansas State Ledger, a Topeka weekly whose local columns addressed its 'colored' readers, called it a 'ridiculous attempt' by armed white men to lynch and told 'black-hearted villains' to let the law take its course.

versions.value: A report given out in the Black churches that whites would lynch Tuttle; testimony traced it to Bob Tuttle's appeal in church
A company of Friends returning from High Point rode through town and was taken for a lynching band
An actual attempt by armed white men to lynch

conflicts.note: The church version comes from the Winston dispatch and sworn trial testimony; the Friends version from a train passenger and a small N.C. weekly; the attempt version from a distant editorial with no detail.
The Salt Lake figure is likely a garble of the 150 wire text; no local count is given.

versions.value: The crowd refused to disperse and fired on the officers
The crowd fired as it, or the officers, were about to leave after an agreement to disperse
Armed white men were the aggressors and colored men resisted

conflicts.note: Every account of the shooting itself comes from officials or white observers; no account from the crowd appears.

versions.value: A rioter who was shot later died ('Another of the negro rioters who was shot is dead')

conflicts.note: The word 'another' implies an earlier death that no report in the coverage records.
The Birmingham headline contradicts its own text; the verdict was second-degree murder.

record_check.dossier: police_violence: militia and deputies fired volleys into an armed Black crowd guarding the jail; no white crowd is reported
No lynching occurred; Tuttle was tried, convicted and sent to the penitentiary. The lynching threat was a rumor officials called untrue; only a distant editorial calls it an attempt
